framework: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biblical Studies (9484) syllabus 2024–2026
subject: Biblical Studies

outcomes.text: Recount Matthew's birth stories (Matthew 1:18-2:23) and how they show Jesus fulfilling Old Testament prophecy.
Recount Luke's birth stories (Luke 1:26-38; 2:1-40) and what they say about who Jesus is.
Explain how the Prologue to John (John 1:1-18) presents Jesus as the Word.
Describe John the Baptist's proclamation (Mark 1:2-8) and the baptism and temptation of Jesus.
Explain the conflict over the Sabbath (Mark 2:23-28) and the rejection at Nazareth.
Explain what happens at Caesarea Philippi and at the transfiguration.
Describe the healing of blind Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46-52) and what it shows about Jesus.
Describe Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem in Mark and John.
Describe the cleansing of the temple in Mark and John and why it caused conflict.
Describe the anointing at Bethany in Mark and John and its meaning.
Describe the healing miracles of the mute man, the unclean spirit and the paralytic, and the reactions to them.
Describe the nature miracles: stilling the storm, feeding the five thousand and walking on water in Mark.
Describe the cure of the blind man at Bethsaida and the centurion's servant (Luke 7:1-10).
Describe the wedding at Cana and the healing of the official's son.
Describe the healing on the Sabbath at the pool (John 5:1-18) and the feeding of the five thousand in John.
Describe Jesus walking on the water and the healing of the man born blind in John.
Tell the story of the raising of Lazarus (John 11:1-44) and why it is the climactic sign.
Explain the sayings 'bread of life' (John 6:35-59) and 'light of the world' (John 8:12).
Explain the sayings 'the gate' and 'the good shepherd' (John 10:1-18).
Explain the sayings 'the resurrection and the life' and 'the way, the truth and the life'.
Explain the saying 'the true vine' (John 15:1-17).
Show understanding of the claims about Jesus' person and the challenges to his authority in the birth and ministry accounts.
Explain the Old Testament, Jewish and Greek background of the titles Christ, Son of Man, Son of God, Son of David and Logos, and judge how fitting they are.
Compare the synoptic miracles with John's seven signs and ask whether John presents Jesus differently.
Interpret the symbolism of the 'I am' sayings and what they teach about Jesus.
Explain the parables of the labourers in the vineyard and the talents and what they teach about God's kingdom.
Explain the seed parables and why Jesus taught in parables (Mark 4).
Explain Jesus' teaching on receiving the kingdom like a child and on wealth (Mark 10:13-31).
Explain Mary's song of praise (Luke 1:46-55) and its view of God.
Explain Jesus' teaching on the kingdom and judgement in Luke 10:8-12.
Explain Jesus' teaching on the goodness of God in Luke 11:9-13.
Explain the parables of the lost sheep, lost coin and the prodigal son and his brother (Luke 15).
Describe Jesus calling Levi and eating with sinners (Mark 2:13-17).
Describe the Syrophoenician woman's faith (Mark 7:24-30).
Describe the forgiveness of the sinful woman (Luke 7:36-50).
Explain the parable of the great dinner (Luke 14:15-24).
Explain the parable of the Pharisee and the tax-collector (Luke 18:9-14).
Describe Jesus and Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1-10).
Describe the woman caught in adultery (John 8:2-11) and Jesus' response.
Explain the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:1-12) and the images of salt and light.
Explain Jesus' teaching on the law and the prophets (Matthew 5:17-48).
Explain Jesus' warnings against showy charity, prayer and fasting (Matthew 6:1-18).
Explain putting God and his kingdom first (Matthew 6:19-34).
Explain Jesus' teaching on judging others and on hearers and doers, the two house-builders.
Explain the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21-35).
Explain the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46).
Explain the request of James and John and Jesus' teaching on service (Mark 10:35-45).
Explain the greatest commandment (Mark 12:28-34) and the new commandment (John 13:34-35).
Explain the good Samaritan and the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 10:25-37; 16:19-31).
Understand the Jewish idea of the kingdom of God, the purpose of parables and Jesus' teaching on God's nature.
Explain why some groups were marginalised in first-century Jewish society and how Jesus treated them.
Judge whether the Sermon on the Mount sets an ideal or an achievable goal for disciples.
Compare the four accounts of the Last Supper.
Compare the accounts of the prediction of Peter's denial.
Compare the accounts of Gethsemane and Jesus' arrest.
Compare the accounts of Jesus before the Sanhedrin.
Compare the accounts of Peter's denials.
Compare the accounts of Jesus before Pilate, including Herod in Luke.
Compare the four crucifixion accounts and their distinctive emphases.
Compare the four accounts of Jesus' burial.
Compare the four accounts of the empty tomb.
Compare the resurrection appearances in all four gospels.
Describe the ascension in Mark and Luke.
Weigh up the similarities and differences in the final-days and resurrection accounts and how each writer's interests shaped them.
Explain the roles of Jesus, the twelve and the Jewish and Roman authorities before the crucifixion.
Consider what the resurrection narratives meant for the evangelists and their communities.

topics.title: 2.1 The origins and expansion of the early church

outcomes.text: Describe Pentecost and the birth of the church (Acts 2:1-13).
Analyse the content and structure of Peter's preaching (Acts 2:14-40; 10:34-43).
Describe how the Jerusalem believers shared wealth and service, such as Barnabas and the seven.
Describe their prayer, worship, baptism, breaking of bread and healing ministry.
Describe Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:1-22).
Describe Stephen's ministry and martyrdom and the persecution of Greek-speaking Jewish Christians.
Describe Saul's part in persecution and his conversion (Acts 9:1-19).
Describe Philip's ministry in Samaria and the baptism of the Ethiopian official.
Explain Peter's vision, the conversion of Cornelius and the Jerusalem church's reaction (Acts 10:1-11:18).
Describe the founding of the mixed church in Syrian Antioch and the ministry of Barnabas and Saul.
Explain Antioch's relationship with Jerusalem and the debate over gentiles (Acts 15:1-35).
Describe the first journey: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.
Describe the second journey: Philippi, Thessalonica, Beroea, Athens and Corinth.
Describe the third journey and events at Ephesus (Acts 19:1-41).
Explain the birth of the church within Judaism and how Christianity emerged as a distinct faith.
Explain the tensions caused within the church by gentile converts.
Judge how successful Paul's three missionary journeys were.
Explain the divisions in Corinth and Paul's response (1 Corinthians 1:10-17; 3:1-4:7).
Explain Paul's teaching on the church as one body and on love (1 Corinthians 12:1-13:13).
Describe the collection for the Jerusalem community (1 Corinthians 16:1-6).
Explain the problem of food offered to idols and Paul's response.
Explain Paul's teaching on relationships, marriage and divorce, and the influence of beliefs about the parousia and gnosticism (1 Corinthians 7).
Explain the passages on women at worship (1 Corinthians 11:2-16; 14:33b-35).
Explain the abuses at the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17-34).
Explain speaking in tongues and Paul's call for orderly worship.
Understand the issues raised by the Corinthians' pagan background.
Identify the key beliefs behind Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians.
Discuss whether Paul's teaching on marriage and on women at worship was local or applies to all Christians.

topics.title: 2.3 The Christian church in the Roman world

outcomes.text: Explain Jesus' warning of persecution (Luke 21:12-19) and the imprisonment of Paul and Silas at Philippi.
Explain the riot of the silversmiths at Ephesus and the cult of Artemis.
Explain 1 Peter's evidence of hostility and its teaching on responding to persecution.
Explain what being God's chosen people meant for 1 Peter's readers.
Use Tacitus' account of Nero's persecution and Pliny's letters to Trajan as non-Christian evidence.
Explain the low status of many Christians, with Onesimus and Philemon.
Explain the centurion's servant (Luke 7:1-10) as a more enlightened slave-owner.
Analyse Paul's views on slavery across Acts, 1 Corinthians, Galatians and Colossians.
Explain 1 Peter's advice to slaves, to wives of non-Christians and to Christian husbands.
Explain why Roman authorities and local people were hostile to Christians.
Understand the situation of the readers of 1 Peter and its teaching.
Judge how far Paul and 1 Peter reflect the outlook of their time on slavery, and whether Paul is unclear.

units.title: Paper 3: Prophets of the Old Testament

outcomes.text: Compare prophecy in the Ancient Near East, such as Mari, with prophecy in Israel.
Discuss whether Israelite prophecy was unique.
Recognise the Hebrew terms roeh, hozeh and nabi and where the set texts use them.
Explain the sons of the prophets as guilds of prophets under a leader.
Explain prophets as inspired by God's spirit, and prophetic ecstasy as contagious.
Explain how prophets were called by God (Moses, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah).
Explain unusual or miraculous births and deaths linked with prophets.
Explain oracles of judgement and oracles of salvation.
Explain visionary experiences, such as Amos 8:1-3.
Explain symbolic acts and signs by Jeremiah and Isaiah.
Explain the prophets' miracles and Nathan's parable.
Explain prophetic intercession for the people.
Explain why true and false prophets were hard to tell apart.
Explain Deuteronomy 18:9-22 on divination and the test of a prophet's word coming true.
Analyse Micaiah's confrontation with Ahab's prophets and the 'lying spirit' (1 Kings 22).
Explain Jeremiah's description of false prophets (Jeremiah 23:9-32).
Show understanding of the nature of Old Testament prophecy against the Ancient Near East.
Understand the different ways prophets delivered their messages.
Consider the issues in telling true prophets from false.

topics.title: 3.2 Early prophets: Samuel, Nathan, Gad and Elijah

outcomes.text: Describe Samuel as a local seer at Ramah and his meeting with Saul (1 Samuel 9:1-10:16).
Explain Samuel's role in choosing Saul, rejecting him and anointing David.
Describe Samuel as military and political leader and judge (1 Samuel 7:3-17).
Discuss whether the portrait of Samuel is historically reliable or idealised.

subtopics.title: Nathan and Gad at David's court

outcomes.text: Explain Nathan's consultation about building a temple (2 Samuel 7).
Explain Nathan's criticism of David over Uriah and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11-12).
Explain Gad's message about David's census (2 Samuel 24).
Explain Elijah as preserver of Yahweh worship against Ahab and Jezebel.
Explain the miracles of the meal and oil, and raising the widow's child.
Explain the contest on Mount Carmel and the ending of the drought.
Explain the dividing of the Jordan and Elijah taken to heaven with his spirit passing to Elisha.
Explain Elijah's confrontation with Ahab over Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21).
Discuss whether the portrait of Elijah is historically reliable or idealised.
Consider Samuel's place in the prophetic tradition and the rise of the monarchy.
Analyse the involvement of Nathan and Gad in the king's court.
Consider Elijah's importance, especially his miracles and conflict with the monarchy.
Discuss how far Samuel and Elijah are historical or idealised portraits.

topics.title: 3.3 Prophecy in national destruction and reconstruction

subtopics.title: Amos and the fall of Samaria

outcomes.text: Explain Amos' condemnation of Israel's social and religious sins.
Explain Amos' confrontation with Amaziah (Amos 7:10-17).
Explain Amos' prophecies of disaster for the Northern Kingdom.
Discuss whether the closing salvation oracle is Amos' own hope or a later editor's.
Explain Jeremiah's call to pluck up and plant (Jeremiah 1).
Explain how Jeremiah's life symbolised coming doom (Jeremiah 16:1-9).
Explain the oracle against Zedekiah and the role of false prophets.
Explain the vision of the good and bad figs (Jeremiah 24).
Explain Jeremiah's confrontation with Hananiah over the length of the exile (Jeremiah 28).
Explain Jeremiah's advice on living in exile and the promise of return (Jeremiah 29; 32:6-15).
Explain the call to announce that the exile is nearly over (Isaiah 40:1-2).
Explain God as Holy One who redeems and restores Israel (Isaiah 43:14-44:5).
Explain Cyrus as God's anointed and the fall of Babylon.
Explain the first Servant Song (Isaiah 42:1-4) and who the servant might be.
Explain the second and third Servant Songs (Isaiah 49:1-6; 50:4-7).
Explain the fourth Servant Song on the suffering servant (Isaiah 52:13-53:12).
Analyse Amos' prophecies of Israel's destruction for its sins.
Analyse the prophecies of exile and restoration in Jeremiah.
Assess the identity of the servant in the Servant Songs and the servant's importance for Israel.

units.title: Paper 4: Christian Understandings of God, Life and the Universe

outcomes.text: Explain creation from nothing by God's word and God as a craftsman shaping existing matter.
Decide whether the two ideas of creation conflict or complement each other.
Study the Genesis 1:1-2:3 creation narrative and its importance in Christian thought.
Study the Genesis 2:4-19 creation narrative and its importance.
Explain other references to God as creator: Psalm 104, John 1:1-4, Acts 17:22-28.
Compare literal, mythical-poetic and metaphorical readings of the creation narratives.
Assess whether similarities with the Enuma Elish and Gilgamesh support or question Genesis.
Assess whether the Big Bang theory is compatible with biblical creation.
Explain how geology and archaeology have challenged traditional readings.
Compare Christian responses: old Earth and young Earth creationists and those who integrate faith and science.
Explain biblical teaching on stewardship (Genesis 2:15; Leviticus 25; Psalm 24).
Explain biblical teaching on dominion (Genesis 1:26-30; 9:1-7; Psalm 8).
Discuss whether Christians should put dominion or stewardship first.
Explain the role of animals in sacrifices under the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants.
Explain the texts that allow people to eat animals.
Explain the biblical arguments for vegetarianism.
Explain Romans 14 on food debates not becoming a stumbling block.
Become familiar with biblical teaching on creation and the views that challenge it.
Understand how beliefs about creation shape views on treating animals and the environment.
Consider the arguments about how animals should or should not be used.
Show understanding of similarity, difference, compatibility and disagreement between texts and interpretations.

subtopics.title: Biblical evidence for life after death

outcomes.text: Explain biblical examples of God going beyond normal life and death: Samuel's shade, Elijah, the transfiguration, Lazarus and the rich man.
Explain Jesus' resurrection and ascension as evidence for life after death.
Compare biblical teaching on bodily resurrection and the immortality of the soul (1 Corinthians 15; 2 Corinthians 4-5; 1 Thessalonians 4-5).
Explain Sheol and Gehenna and the texts that use them.
Explain Hades and the biblical ideas of heaven and hell.
Explain the four New Testament ideas on how salvation is gained: law, works, faith and grace.
Show how Acts 15, Romans 2-5, Galatians, Ephesians 2, James 2 and 1 John 2 address these ideas.
Discuss whether the four ideas complement or contradict each other.
Become familiar with the meanings of biblical terms about life after death and salvation.
Consider the different pictures of life after death in the Bible.
Show how different teachings on salvation have influenced Christians.
Show understanding of similarity, difference, compatibility and disagreement between texts.
Explain God as omnipotent through Psalm 33, Job 42 and Daniel 4.
Explain God as omnibenevolent through Psalm 33, John 3 and 1 John 4.
Explain God as omniscient through Psalm 33, Psalm 139 and Matthew 10.

subtopics.title: The problem of evil and theodicies

outcomes.text: Explain the problem of evil, including Mackie's inconsistent triad.
Explain Augustine's theodicy and one scholarly criticism of it.
Explain the Irenaean theodicy of John Hick and one scholarly criticism of it.
Explain how Job 1-2 establishes Job's righteousness and his undeserved suffering.
Explain the dialogues between Yahweh and Satan about Job.
Explain how Job responds to his suffering and turmoil in Job 3.
Explain the arguments of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar about Job's suffering.
Explain how Job answers his friends.
Explain what the dialogues show about the cause and purpose of suffering.

subtopics.title: Job and the limits of understanding

outcomes.text: Explain Elihu's rebuke of Job and his friends (Job 35-37).
Explain Yahweh's rebuke of Job (Job 38:1-40:14).
Explain Job's acceptance in Job 42 as a possible biblical theodicy.
Show understanding of the Irenaean and Augustinian theodicies.
Explain the ancient question of reconciling a loving God with suffering.
Consider Job as a study of the problem of suffering.
Analyse the conclusions of the theodicies and of Job.
Show understanding of similarity, difference, compatibility and disagreement between texts.
